tweets.text: RT @NetChoice: Another NetChoice Victory for Free Speech & Families: Fifth Circuit Keeps A Texas Online Censorship Law Blocked NEW ORLEANS—The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit today affirmed the injunction blocking the central censorship requirement of Texas's HB 18, the so-called SCOPE Act. The ruling keeps the government from dictating what lawful speech Texas families see online, and leaves that decision with parents, where it belongs. "This is a win for every Texan who believes the government has no business deciding what they can read, watch, and say online," said @Paul_Taske, Director of the NetChoice Litigation Center. "HB 18 would have forced websites to censor broad, vaguely defined categories of lawful speech. The Fifth Circuit is right to keep it blocked. Parents, not the government, are best positioned to decide what is appropriate for their own families, and today's ruling protects that fundamental right." Today's decision continues a clear national trend: courts have now blocked similar online censorship and age-gating laws in California, Arkansas, and Mississippi. An unconstitutional law protects no one, and HB 18 is no exception. Texas families are best served by real safety tools that respect the Constitution, like NetChoice’s Digital Safety Shield for America. NetChoice is confident these censorship requirements will be struck down for good as the case moves forward.

tweets.text: RT @WatcherGuru: President Donald Trump's $1.4 billion earnings from his crypto ventures has become a major obstacle in Senate negotiations over the Clarity Act. Senate Republicans introduced revised language this week in an effort to end a months-long stalemate. Democrats and consumer watchdog groups quickly rejected the proposal, arguing that it does not include strong enough safeguards to prevent a sitting president or members of the president’s family from profiting from crypto businesses while the administration regulates the same industry. The dispute centers on Trump's memecoin and other family-linked crypto ventures, which critics say raise potential conflict-of-interest concerns. The disagreement could further delay legislation designed to clarify how cryptocurrencies and other digital assets are regulated in the United States.
